name: Lash growth serum (peptide)

lead: Lash serums are cosmetic liquids brushed along the upper lash line to make lashes look longer and fuller. Peptide versions are sold over the counter as an alternative to prescription prostaglandin products.

Brands say peptides condition and support lashes. The trial-level information in the sources covers bimatoprost (Latisse), whose manufacturer reports visible growth within 16 weeks and up to about 25 percent more length; no published human trials of peptide serums were found.

paras: People apply the serum along the base of the upper lashes, typically nightly, and keep using it for weeks while watching for changes. Some layer it with mascara or lash curling for added definition.
Peptide serums are sold as cosmetics and can cause irritation or allergy near the eye. For bimatoprost, reported effects include infection from reused applicators and eyelid darkening.

angle.text: Users apply over-the-counter peptide serums to the lash line for longer, fuller-looking lashes without a prescription. Brands say the peptides condition and support the lash. The prescription product bimatoprost has trial data; trials of the peptide versions were not found.

lead: Peptide lash growth serums are over-the-counter cosmetic liquids brushed along the upper lash line, sold with the aim of making lashes look longer, fuller and darker over a few weeks. They are an alternative to the prescription prostaglandin product Latisse (bimatoprost), and some brands choose peptides over prostaglandin analogues because of regulatory rules in places such as Canada and California.[1]

People use them to improve the frame around the eyes. Longer, denser, more curved lashes make the eyes read as larger and more defined without mascara, curlers or salon extensions, and the effect is on the person's own lashes rather than an attachment. Follicle number is set before birth, so any serum can act only on the lashes a person already has.[1]

Research is uneven across the category. Bimatoprost has a large trial record for eyelash hypotrichosis, including randomized studies in adults, post-chemotherapy patients, Japanese participants and children.[2][3][4][5][6] For peptide products, a 2024 open-label trial of a peptide and glycosaminoglycan serum in 30 women reported gains in lash structure over 12 weeks.[7] A 2026 analysis of 79 marketed lash serums found that about 30 percent contained a prostaglandin analogue, while the rest relied on ingredients such as castor oil, amino acids, panthenol and peptides.[8]
infobox: Applied at the base of the lashes
Peptides, often with conditioning agents such as panthenol, amino acids or oils
Cosmetic (OTC); prostaglandin-containing serums are regulated differently

paras: A lash serum is a thin hydroalcoholic or water-based liquid applied with a small brush along the upper lash line, usually once daily, with results discussed over weeks to months. A 2026 survey of 79 products found most were hydroalcoholic solutions.[8] Peptide serums typically combine short-chain peptides with moisturising or conditioning ingredients and are marketed for strength, density and shine of the lash fibre.[7][8]

Peptide products sit alongside other lash options: mascara, curlers and perms change the look of lashes without lengthening them, extensions are bonded to the lid, tints darken the lashes, and lash transplants use scalp hair that keeps growing and needs trimming.[1][9]

Eyelash length is largely genetic. Upper lashes typically measure about 3 to 10 mm (usually 7 to 8 mm) and lower lashes about 5 to 6 mm; an upper lid carries roughly 90 to 160 lashes and a lower lid 75 to 80.[1] Follicles form during embryonic development, so their number cannot rise after birth, and lashes regrow in roughly seven to eight weeks after plucking.[1]

Bimatoprost is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue approved in the US for glaucoma in 2001 under the brand Lumigan. Allergan launched Latisse in early 2009 as the first FDA-approved lash-growth drug, with the company reporting visible growth within 16 weeks, mainly on the upper lashes, and up to about 25 percent more length.[1][10] The cosmetic form is applied at the lash base rather than instilled in the eye, and it is also sold as Careprost and Mylash in some markets.[10]

A reference work states that some brands choose peptides because of regulatory rules in places such as Canada and California; that statement rests on a retailer blog post, and the specific rules are not detailed there.[1] The 2026 survey authors report that prostaglandin analogues, including bimatoprost, norbimatoprost, ethyl tafluprostamide and isopropyl cloprostenate, are found in some lash serums sold as cosmetics even though they are not regulated for cosmetic use, which they say creates several problems.[8]

Cosmetic companies also cite research on prostaglandin and Wnt/beta-catenin signalling in hair growth when describing how lash products might work; manufacturers of peptide serums describe their ingredients as supporting the lash fibre and follicle rather than acting as drugs.[1][7]

Peptide serums: a 2024 open-label trial enrolled 30 women aged 25 to 65 and applied a serum containing peptides and glycosaminoglycans, assessing lashes at baseline, week 4 and week 12 with image-analysis software. By week 12 all measured parameters had risen from baseline, with the largest gain in lash angle (about 28 percent) and smaller gains in length and number; satisfaction rose from about 73 percent at week 4 to about 84 percent at week 12, and no adverse effects were reported. The trial had no control group.[7]

Bimatoprost: randomized, double-masked trials have examined 0.03 percent bimatoprost for eyelash hypotrichosis in adults, in people who had lost lashes to chemotherapy, in Japanese participants, in children and for patient-reported outcomes, and a pooled analysis combined six such trials for safety.[2][11][3][4][5][6] A retrospective review looked at long-term satisfaction and use patterns, and a small pilot examined the same drug on eyebrows.[12][13] A 2011 review compared prescription and over-the-counter options for enhancing lashes.[9]
Reference works note that bimatoprost works on healthy lashes while its effect on lash loss from alopecia areata is debated.[1]

The most common effect of ophthalmic bimatoprost is eye redness (over 10 percent of patients); permanent iris darkening is a known effect of the eye-drop form. For the cosmetic lash form, reported concerns include infection if single-use applicators are reused and darkening of eyelid skin.[10] The 2024 peptide trial reported no adverse effects in its 30 participants.[7]

Regulatory treatment differs by product: bimatoprost is prescription-only in the US and EU, while peptide serums are sold as cosmetics.[10][8] The 2026 survey authors flag prostaglandin analogues in cosmetic serums as an area of concern.[8]

On looksmax.org, members ask which lash serum to try and compare Latisse, a water-based serum from The Ordinary, and oils such as castor and rosemary, and ask how long results take. Latisse is the reference point they usually compare cosmetic serums against. Lash density and curl are discussed as part of eye-area aesthetics alongside brow and under-eye topics.

lore.intro: Lash serums are discussed on looksmax.org as a low-effort way to improve the eye area; members compare Latisse with peptide and oil-based alternatives and swap experiences on timing.
